places.name: Trạc Anh Đài
places.look: A low wooded rise above a clear, cold stream, its halls stepping up in grey-tiled tiers among birch and fir. At its foot lies the terrace that gives the sect its name: a broad granite platform running out into the water, strung with long bamboo poles where rows of dyed hat strings hang drying in the wind.
places.lore: Fishers and sea hunters of the frost coast keep this small sect (tông môn) of body cultivators (thể tu), sworn to Băng Tâm Các; its head is Đoàn Thanh Lãng, born in Liên Giang Thành. Every new disciple washes the strings of a reed hat on the terrace on the day they join, after the old fisherman's song: when the water is clear, wash your hat strings in it. When a thaw muddies the stream, no oath is sworn until it runs clear again.
places.history: Until 498 the frost coast belonged to Hàn Giang Môn, whose fishers cultivated alone in the snow on the cold river. When Băng Tâm Các took the coast that year, the fishers stayed and worked on under the Pavilion's flag, keeping the old habits but no sect of their own. In 830 fishers and sea hunters of the frost coast founded Trạc Anh Đài on this rise, sworn to Băng Tâm Các as their lord. The founders chose the place for its stream, which runs clear even in the spring floods, and built the washing terrace before any hall. They trained the body rather than the sword, hardening hunters for the winter sea and the ice floes. The woodcutters of Tiều Lộ Thôn came to answer to the terrace. In 990 Đoàn Thanh Lãng was born in Liên Giang Thành during a cold rain that joined the river by night; he leads the terrace now.
places.art_brief: A small vertical sect seat on a low wooded rise: a few tiers of grey-tile roofs over pale cedar walls climbing among snow-dusted birch and fir, the top hall the tallest outline around it. At the base a broad, flat granite terrace runs into a clear pale-green stream, with rows of thin bamboo poles hung with tiny threads of red, indigo and ochre cord. Warm golden light from the top left, long blue shadows on thin snow. No text, no people larger than specks, no coastline or boats, nothing beyond the rise and the stream bank.
levels: A second terrace is cut lower into the stream, a covered hall rises at the crest, and smokehouses for seal meat line the path up the rise.
The halls reach the crest under a tall watch pavilion, a stone stair joins every terrace, and the drying poles stretch in long bright rows down both banks.

places.name: Liên Giang Thành
places.look: A grey port city where a cold river meets the sea, its walls running down both banks to the harbour. Across the river mouth stretches a long roofed bridge of dark timber and grey tile, its eaves hung with racks of silver ice-fish drying in the rain.
places.lore: The fishers of Hàn Giang Môn built the city and it still smells of their trade; under Băng Tâm Các its people pay their tax in ice-fish, as they have since the frost coast fell. Cold rain comes in off the sea at night and joins the river, and locals say a child born in such a rain will never drown; Đoàn Thanh Lãng, head of Trạc Anh Đài, was born on such a night. The city's line is the first of Băng Tâm's own poem: cold rain joins the river by night.
places.history: Hàn Giang Môn founded Liên Giang Thành in 350, where the cold rain joins the river, as the harbour of its fisher cultivators (tu sĩ). For a century and a half its boats worked the cold river and the frost coast under the Gate of the Cold River. In the last years of the Age of Seven Seats Băng Tâm Các made war on Hàn Giang for the coast, and in 498 Hàn Giang fell with its last head Liễu Cô Chu; the city passed to the Pavilion with the rest of Hàn Sương Châu. From 499 the old sect's fishers kept fishing the cold river under Băng Tâm's flag and paid their tax in ice-fish, a custom still kept. Old people say the roofed bridge was raised in Hàn Giang's time so the fishers could mend nets out of the rain. In 990 Đoàn Thanh Lãng was born here during a cold rain that joined the river by night, and grew up to lead Trạc Anh Đài. Today the city is the frost coast's oldest port and Băng Tâm's door to the sea.
places.art_brief: A city miniature at a river mouth on a forested coast: rectangular grey stone walls running down both banks, dense grey-tile roofs inside, a small harbour of fishing boats. The signature is a long, low roofed bridge of dark timber spanning the river mouth, its eaves lined with tiny silver racks of drying fish. Dark firs at the city's back, cold slate-blue water, a thin veil of rain over the sea edge. Warm golden light from the top left catching the wet roofs. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the walls and the bridge.
levels: The roofed bridge is doubled with a second span, new ice-houses line the quays, and the walls take in the fishers' quarter on the far bank.
A tall grey drum tower rises over the harbour, the quays run out in stone piers to the sea, and both banks are walled to the forest edge.

places.name: Tống Khách Thị
places.look: A forest market strung along the road on a gentle rise, its stalls tucked under dark fir eaves. At the eastern end stands a small eight-sided farewell pavilion over a stone table, where a single cup is always set out full.
places.lore: Travellers leaving the frost coast are seen off here at dawn, and the market lives on what they buy for the road: furs, dried fish and warm wine. Since a traveller seen off in 900 never returned, the market pours a farewell cup for him at the pavilion every year. The wandering sword sage Tư Không Hạc Niên, bound to no sect, has lived here since his duel of 1130 and teaches no one, however many come to ask.
places.history: Tống Khách Thị grew where the frost coast's road climbs inland, the last place travellers on Băng Tâm's roads took a cup before the long way south. Its name comes from the Băng Tâm poem: at dawn I see my guest off. In 900 a traveller was seen off from the market at dawn and never returned; the record keeps no name for him, and the market has poured a farewell cup for him every year since. The eight-sided pavilion at the eastern end was built, the stallholders say, to keep that cup out of the snow. In 1130, after his three-day duel with Thang Vô Tạ of Phất Y Cốc on Cùng Mục Phong ended with no winner, the wandering sword sage Tư Không Hạc Niên settled here. He teaches no one, though young swordsmen come up the road every year to ask. The market has grown used to him, and he to the market.
places.art_brief: A low cluster of grey-tile stall roofs strung along a pale road on a gentle forested rise, timber posts and fur-hung awnings, dark firs close on both sides. At the eastern end a small eight-sided pavilion with an upturned grey roof sits over a tiny stone table, its single cup a speck of white. Light snow on the eaves, warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing beyond the road's edge.
levels: A walled inn yard joins the market, and the stalls double along the road under longer eaves.
The market gains a gate and a covered street, and a second, larger pavilion rises beside the old one, which is kept exactly as it was.

places.name: Mộc Lan Thành
places.look: A walled harbour city on the flat frost coast, its grey roofs low against the sea wind. A double row of old magnolia trees runs the length of the harbour wall, and in spring their white blossoms line the quay like snow that will not melt. Inland, the white cone of Sương Diễm Sơn stands over the city.
places.lore: Băng Tâm Các's younger port on the frost coast trades furs, timber and live beasts from Vô Tung Lâm; hunters sell their catches on the magnolia quay, and buyers come from as far as Thiên Bảo Trai. The city remembers the week in the Age of the North Star Compact when Sương Diễm Sơn breathed fire and everyone slept on the beach; on that night each year, families still lay their bedding out on the sand.
places.history: Băng Tâm Các founded Mộc Lan Thành on the frost coast in 620, more than a century after taking Hàn Sương Châu from Hàn Giang Môn. Its builders planted magnolias along the new harbour wall, a southern tree coaxed to bloom in the cold, and the city took its name from them. Within a century of the founding, Sương Diễm Sơn breathed fire under the frost for a week, and the people of Mộc Lan Thành slept on the beach until it sank. The city grew as the coast's market for the furs and timber of Vô Tung Lâm, a forest only the coast's woodcutters and hunters dare. In 1180 hunters brought a white bear out of Vô Tung Lâm alive and sold it here to a buyer from Thiên Bảo Trai. The tale of that bear's long road south is still told in the harbour taverns. Today the city lives by the sea and the forest at once.
places.art_brief: A city miniature on a flat, fir-edged coast: low rectangular grey walls, grey-tile roofs pressed close, a small harbour with a stone quay. Along the harbour wall runs a double line of small round trees covered in white blossom, the brightest white in the scene. A strip of pale beach to one side. Warm golden light from the top left, cool blue sea. No text, no people larger than specks, no volcano inside the footprint, nothing outside the walls and quay.
levels: A fur market hall with a high grey roof rises behind the quay, and the magnolia rows run on along a new sea wall.
The walls take in the beach quarter, a stone breakwater shelters the harbour, and a three-roofed gate tower faces the volcano inland.

places.name: Kê Minh Trấn
places.look: A small walled port town on the grassy frost coast, low grey roofs around a single harbour. Above its gate stands a tall pole topped by a bronze rooster, green with age, that turns with the wind.
places.lore: The cocks of Kê Minh crow even in the dark of winter, when the sun barely rises, and the town has kept the cock as its emblem since the Age of Seven Seats (Thất Tọa Kỷ). Its fishers set out at the first crow, not the first light, and a household whose cock falls silent fetches a new one before nightfall.
places.history: Kê Minh grew on the grassy frost coast as a fishing harbour in the days of Hàn Giang Môn. By 360 its cocks were known to crow even in the dark of winter, when the sun barely clears the sea, and the town took the cock as its emblem. Its fishers learned to set out at the first crow rather than the first light, and its boats were the first on the water all along the coast. When Hàn Giang Môn fell and the frost coast passed to Băng Tâm Các at the end of the Age of Seven Seats, the town changed its flag but not its emblem. The bronze rooster above the gate was cast, the townsfolk say, to go on crowing if every bird in the town ever fell silent. They boast that no bad news has ever reached Kê Minh before the first crow.
places.art_brief: A low town miniature on a grassy coast: a small rectangular wall of grey stone, a tight cluster of grey-tile roofs, a short harbour wall with a few boats. Over the gate a tall thin pole carries a tiny verdigris-green rooster, the highest point of the town. Pale winter grass, cold sea. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the walls and harbour.
levels: The harbour wall is lengthened into a stone pier and a fish market roof rises by the gate.
A second ring of wall takes in the poultry yards and net sheds, and a covered gatehouse lifts the rooster pole higher still.

places.name: Tiều Lộ Thôn
places.look: A woodcutters' village where the forest comes down to the shore, its log houses under grey-tile roofs around a small timber jetty. At the forest's edge a fan of red-painted marker posts leads off among the trees, each one the start of a different path into Vô Tung Lâm.
places.lore: The woodcutters' paths into Vô Tung Lâm vanish under the snow every night, and only the people of Tiều Lộ Thôn can find them again; outsiders who need the forest hire a Tiều Lộ guide or go without. The village answers to Trạc Anh Đài, and it is said the poles of the terrace's drying lines are cut by Tiều Lộ hands.
places.history: Woodcutters settled this shore where Vô Tung Lâm comes down to the sea, cutting timber for the boats of the frost coast. By 540 their paths into the forest were known to vanish under the snow every night, and only the people of Tiều Lộ Thôn could find them again. They marked the start of each path with a painted post and kept the rest of the way in their heads, passed from parent to child. Hunters and timber buyers from the coast's towns learned to hire a Tiều Lộ guide or stay out of the trees. When the fishers and sea hunters of the coast founded Trạc Anh Đài, the village came under the terrace's hand, and it is said Tiều Lộ's woodcutters cut the poles for the terrace's drying lines. The elders boast that the village has never lost a guide in the forest, though it has lost many who went in without one.
places.art_brief: A small village miniature on a forested shore: a few log houses with grey-tile roofs, stacked cordwood, a short timber jetty into cold water. At the tree line behind, a spread fan of tiny red posts runs into the snowy firs. Warm golden light from the top left, snow on the roofs. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the village and its edge of forest.
levels: A sawpit and a log slide down to the jetty, and more houses climb along the posts toward the trees.
A palisade circles the village, a covered timber yard faces the water, and the red posts gain carved caps for each family's path.

places.name: Lâm Ẩn Thôn
places.look: A coastal village so deep in old firs that from the sea only its chimney smoke shows above the canopy. A single long plank jetty runs out of the trees into a quiet inlet.
places.lore: In the Age of the North Star Compact (Bắc Thần Kỷ) a hermit sheltered here and taught the village children to read tracks in the snow, and every child of Lâm Ẩn still learns tracks before letters. Hunters from Mộc Lan Thành come to hire them, and it is said no beast passes near the village without being named by its footprints.
places.history: Lâm Ẩn Thôn grew in a stand of old firs on the frost coast, so deep in the trees that passing boats saw only its smoke. Its people lived by fishing the inlet and hunting the forest edge. In 780 the village sheltered a hermit who taught its children to read tracks in the snow; the record keeps no name for him. He stayed until the children could tell a fox from a marten by a single print, and then, the villagers say, he walked into the forest and left no track at all. Every child of Lâm Ẩn has learned tracks before letters ever since. Hunters from Mộc Lan Thành come to hire them, and Băng Tâm's patrols ask a Lâm Ẩn tracker first when something goes missing in the woods.
places.art_brief: A natural-looking patch of dense, dark old firs on a coast, the grey-tile roofs only glimpsed between trunks; several thin threads of chimney smoke rise straight out of the canopy. A single long, narrow plank jetty runs from the trees into a still blue inlet. Snow on the fir crowns, warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, no clearings, nothing outside the stand of firs and the jetty.
levels: A tracking lodge is built under the firs and a second jetty reaches the inlet.
The village grows a hidden ring of houses under the canopy, a smokehouse row along the shore, and a small hall where the children learn the tracks.

places.name: Lô Hoa Thôn
places.look: A marsh village on the grassy coast, its stilt houses standing in a sea of reeds. In summer the reeds flower white and the whole marsh looks snowed over, with only grey roofs and winding boat channels showing through.
places.lore: The people of Lô Hoa cut reeds for thatch, mats and net floats, and sell the reed-flower down the coast to Liên Giang and Mộc Lan for stuffing winter quilts. Children are told the summer snow is the frost coast's reminder that winter is never far away.
places.history: Reed-cutters built their stilt houses in this coastal marsh, where the reeds grow tall enough to hide a boat and the spring thaw floods the ground. From the first they cut reeds for thatch, mats and the floats of nets. In 640 the reed flowers covered the marsh like snow in summer, and the sight drew travellers from along the coast. The village learned to sell the soft reed-flower for stuffing winter quilts, and the white summers made its name. Its reeds and down now go by boat to the ports of Liên Giang and Mộc Lan. Each summer, when the marsh first turns white, the children run the plank walks shouting that the snow has come early.
places.art_brief: A village miniature in a coastal marsh: a handful of small grey-tile roofs on timber stilts, joined by plank walks, standing in a dense field of reeds topped with soft white plumes, with dark winding water channels cut through it. Warm golden light from the top left makes the plumes glow cream. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the marsh.
levels: A reed-drying yard on stilts and a boat shed are added, and the plank walks reach a new row of houses.
A raised earth bank with a small grey-tile hall rises in the marsh, and the channels are lined with posts for the reed boats.

places.name: Băng Lăng Khoáng
places.look: A mine mouth high on a bare grey mountainside, a timber headframe and spoil heaps under snow. Over the adit hangs a curtain of icicles thick as a man, which the miners walk through and never break.
places.lore: Băng Tâm Các opened the mine in 580 for the cold metal in its rock; the shafts are hung with ice that never melts, even beside the miners' lamps. Miners wrap their boots in felt and speak softly underground, believing a shout can bring the ice down on them.
places.history: Băng Tâm Các took the frost land at the end of the Age of Seven Seats and searched its mountains for cold metal for its swords. In 580 it opened Băng Lăng Khoáng, a shaft hung with ice that never melts. The miners found that the ice grew back wherever it was broken, and learned to walk through the curtain of icicles at the mouth without touching it. Its cold metal went down the mountain to the Pavilion's sword smiths. The miners took to wrapping their boots in felt and speaking softly underground, believing a shout can bring the ice down. No one has ever seen the ice melt, even beside the lamps, and the mine is still worked today.
places.art_brief: A small mine miniature on a steep grey mountain slope: a dark rectangular adit framed in timber, hung across its mouth with a dense curtain of long blue-white icicles; a timber headframe and grey spoil heaps beside it, snow on everything. Warm golden light from the top left glinting on the ice. No text, no people larger than specks, no buildings beyond a small shed, nothing outside the slope.

places.name: Sương Diễm Sơn
places.look: A broad snow-capped volcanic cone rising alone out of the forest. Down one flank runs a crimson fissure that never freezes, glowing through the snow and trailing a thin plume of steam.
places.lore: No sect holds the mountain; the fire under its frost draws cultivators of both fire and water to its slopes, each sure the other side's qi is the danger. The people of Mộc Lan Thành watch its steam the way sailors watch the sky.
places.history: Sương Diễm Sơn smoked under its snow long before any sect came to the north-east, and the fishers of Hàn Giang Môn called it the mountain of frost and flame. It stood outside every border when Băng Tâm Các took the frost coast in 498, and the Pavilion has never claimed it. In the Age of the North Star Compact Băng Tâm founded Mộc Lan Thành on the coast below it. In 700 the mountain breathed fire under the frost for a week, and the people of Mộc Lan Thành slept on the beach until the fire sank. Ash fell on the snow that winter, and the forest at its foot grew thick and dark in the years after. The crimson fissure on its flank has never closed since. Wandering cultivators climb to it to temper fire and water arts together, though few stay long.
places.art_brief: A natural site: a broad, solitary volcanic cone with a white snow cap, ringed at its base by dark firs; one flank split by a narrow glowing crimson fissure from which a thin white steam plume drifts. No buildings, no roofline. Warm golden light from the top left on the snow, the fissure glowing against the shadow side. No text, no people, nothing outside the cone and its forest skirt.

places.name: Phiến Băng Hồ
places.look: A small round lake set in a hollow of the forest. In winter it freezes as clear as glass, so the stones and weed of its bed show through the ice, and the dark specks of meditating disciples sit scattered across it like drops of ink.
places.lore: The lake lies near Băng Tâm Các, and its name comes from a line of the Pavilion's poem: one piece of ice heart. Since the winter of 1065, when it froze clear as glass and disciples who meditated on it saw their own hearts, Băng Tâm disciples walk out onto it each winter to sit. Its qi runs to wood and fire, strangely warm for a frozen lake, and the elders say that is why it shows a heart and not a face.
places.history: The lake has no recorded name from before Băng Tâm Các came to the cold north-east in the Age of Seven Seats. The Pavilion named it Phiến Băng Hồ after a line of its poem, one piece of ice heart. For centuries it froze white and cloudy like any forest lake. In 1065 it froze as clear as glass, and Băng Tâm disciples who meditated on it saw their own hearts. Since that winter disciples have gone out onto the ice every year; some come back calmer, and some come back and leave the sect. No one holds the lake, but no one fishes it. Elders of the Pavilion hold that the clear ice comes only in winters when the Pavilion's own heart is steady.
places.art_brief: A natural site: a small round lake in a forest hollow, frozen perfectly clear so the brown stones and green weed of its bed show through glassy ice; a few tiny dark specks of seated figures scattered on the ice. Dark firs and snow on the rim. No buildings, no roofline. Warm golden light from the top left glancing off the ice. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the hollow.

places.name: Vô Tung Lâm
places.look: A dark, rolling forest of spruce and fir under deep snow, its crowns bowed white. Through it runs a frozen stream like a white ribbon, and not one track crosses it or the snow on either bank.
places.lore: The Forest Without Tracks takes its name from the poem: on ten thousand paths, no human trace. Snow fills every path by morning and only the woodcutters of Tiều Lộ Thôn can find the ways again; white bears, snow foxes and stranger beasts live deep inside. Hunters who go in alone notch the trees behind them, and still come back mostly by luck.
places.history: No sect has ever claimed the forest, and no road crosses it. In the Age of Seven Seats the fishers of Hàn Giang Môn cut wood at its edge but never went deep. Early in the Age of the North Star Compact the woodcutters' paths into it were known to vanish under the snow every night, and only the people of Tiều Lộ Thôn could find them again. After Băng Tâm Các founded Mộc Lan Thành on the coast, the forest's timber and furs fed the city's market. Late in the same age a hermit sheltering at Lâm Ẩn Thôn, on the coast at the forest's edge, taught the village children to read its beasts' tracks in the snow. In the last generation of the Age of Vein Wars hunters brought a white bear out of Vô Tung Lâm alive and sold it in Mộc Lan Thành to a buyer from Thiên Bảo Trai, and the forest's beasts have had a price on the coast ever since. Still, no map shows its heart.
places.art_brief: A natural site: a dense, rolling mass of dark spruce and fir with snow-laden crowns, no clearings, cut through by a single winding frozen stream that lies like a smooth white ribbon with untouched snow on both banks. No buildings, no roofline, no paths. Warm golden light from the top left on the crowns, deep blue shadow between trees. No text, no people, nothing outside the forest.

places.name: Hàn Giang Môn
places.look: A broken sect seat on the frost coast: a stone gate arch fallen on its side and half buried in snow, behind it the stumps of halls stepping up a low bank. A fishing rod carved along the fallen lintel shows where the wind has swept the snow away.
places.lore: Here the Gate of the Cold River taught its fishers to cultivate alone in the snow beside holes cut in the river ice, sitting for days without moving. It fell to Băng Tâm Các in 498 with its last head Liễu Cô Chu. The coast's fishers still leave a fish on the fallen gate after a good catch, and no one, not even Băng Tâm's disciples, takes it.
places.history: Liễu Thoa Lạp founded Hàn Giang Môn on the frost coast in 300, a sect of fishers who cultivated alone in the snow on the cold river. By 330 its fishers were known for cutting holes in the river ice and sitting beside them in the snow for days without moving. A generation later the sect founded Liên Giang Thành where the cold rain joins the river. When Băng Tâm Các came to the cold north-east in the Age of Seven Seats, the two sects shared the ice uneasily. Half a century later Băng Tâm, under Tần Ngưng Sương, made war on Hàn Giang for the frost coast. In 498 Hàn Giang Môn fell with its last head Liễu Cô Chu, and Hàn Sương Châu passed to Băng Tâm Các. Its fishers stayed and fished the cold river under the Pavilion's flag, but the seat was never rebuilt, and the snow has had it since.
places.art_brief: A ruin miniature on a low snowy coastal bank: broken stone stumps of halls in small terraces, a few jagged wall ends and one leaning timber post as broken verticals; in front, a large stone gate arch lying on its side, half buried in snow, a long carved rod visible along its lintel. Dark firs behind, grey sea in front. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people, no intact roofs, nothing outside the ruin's footprint.

places.name: Tuyết Lang Nguyên
places.look: Open tundra on a low rise, flat and white under a wide sky. Across it runs a low ridge of frost-split grey boulders, the dark mouths of wolf dens between them and trampled snow all around.
places.lore: Snow wolves run here in packs; no sect holds the plain and no road crosses it. Frost-coast hunters say the packs answer to an old grey she-wolf never seen in daylight, and they hunt only the plain's edges in winter and leave the ridge alone.
places.art_brief: A natural site: flat pale tundra with sparse brown grass under snow, crossed by a low ridge of cracked grey boulders with small dark den openings and trampled paths in the snow around them. No buildings, no roofline. Warm golden light from the top left, long shadows from the boulders. No text, no creatures larger than specks, nothing outside the rise.

places.name: Noãn Ngọc Tuyền
places.look: High in the snowy mountains, a chain of steaming pools spills down a rocky slope. The stones around them are a pale jade green and warm to the touch, and snow never settles on them.
places.lore: Băng Tâm Các holds the spring, and its disciples come here to warm meridians numbed by long ice cultivation. Mountain folk say the stones are the bones of a fire beast sleeping under Hàn Sương Châu, the same that wakes in Sương Diễm Sơn; the Pavilion neither confirms nor denies it.
places.art_brief: A natural site: a stepped chain of small steaming pools on a rocky mountain slope, rimmed with smooth pale jade-green stones that stay bare while snow covers everything around them; soft white steam drifting up. No buildings, no roofline. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the slope.

places.name: Khách Tương Đường
places.look: A low green headland over the strait carries halls rising in grey-tile tiers to one high hall, now a hostel for travellers. On the point stands a tall mast hung with green lanterns, lit every dusk, and below it the ferries come and go from the quay.
places.lore: Khách Tương Đường, the Strangers' Hall, is the old seat of Bình Thủy Môn, the sect of the strait crossing, which moved to its Tide Hall on Cự Ngao Chử in 1116. Newcomers sleep their first night here, free, and are fed before they are asked anything. The Book of Meetings, in which every newcomer writes the name of their home village, is kept here by the purser Cù Bối Ngân, and the mast still carries the homes of all who have served. Strangers far from home founded the sect on this headland in 520.
places.history: A generation before the sect, Cô Vụ Đảo became Lạc Hà Tông's land when Giang Bích Không swore Cô Phàm Các to Lạc Hà in the Strait Oath. In 520 strangers far from home, who had met on the island like duckweed on water, founded Bình Thủy Môn on this headland. In 525 a market of chance meetings, Tương Phùng Thị, grew up at the quay below the seat, and the sect's ferries made it the island's door to the mainland. When the fleet of Cô Phàm Các was lost at sea in the Age of the North Star Compact, Bình Thủy's ferries became the island's surest ships. In the Age of Vein Wars Wave Rock split at Lãng Thạch Thôn, one of the sect's villages, and gave up a sea cave of old Cô Phàm charts; some say the best of them are kept in the seat's archive. In 1110 Bùi Phiêu Bình became head, and under him the strait crossing runs every day of the year, storm or calm.
places.art_brief: A vertical sect seat on a low grassy headland: grey-tile pagoda roofs and pale walls stepping up the slope to one high hall, the tallest outline on this coast. On the tip of the headland a tall slender mast hung with many tiny green lanterns. At the foot a stone stair down to a small quay. Turquoise strait water, warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, no market rafts, nothing outside the headland.
levels: A ferry hall rises by the quay, and a second tier of halls climbs the headland behind the main hall.
The headland is terraced to the point, a covered stair runs down to a stone pier, and the lantern mast is doubled with a second mast across the cove.

places.name: Đàm Ảnh Thành
places.look: A low walled port city on the island's grassy shore where a river meets the sea. In its heart lies a large round pool, so still that the clouds and the city's roofs lie upside down in it, ringed with open pavilions where painters set up their easels.
places.lore: Cô Phàm Các built the city in 410 and it outlived the sect; now it is Lạc Hà Tông's, and lives by fish, trade and painters. Painters come from the mainland to paint the sky upside down in the pool, and a painting made here is signed at the bottom, not the top. The blind Đoạn Thương Hải, who survived the Hóa Thần tribulation (thiên kiếp) that killed his master, has lived beside the pool since 1062 and listens to it instead of looking at it.
places.history: Cô Phàm Các, the sailors' sect of Cô Vụ Đảo, founded only a decade before, built Đàm Ảnh Thành in 410, and below it the harbour of Bích Không Cảng, from which its sails vanished into the blue. At the close of the Age of Seven Seats the Strait Oath swore Cô Phàm Các to Lạc Hà Tông. Nearly three centuries after the city's founding a storm sank the whole Cô Phàm fleet with its head Mã Viễn Ảnh, and the city lost its masters in a night; Lạc Hà's stewards took it in hand. A year later the harbour below was abandoned, and the city turned to its river quay and its pool. By 800 the pool mirrored the clouds so clearly that painters came from the mainland to paint the sky upside down. In 1060 a Hóa Thần tribulation over the island sea killed the master of Đoạn Thương Hải, who survived it blind, holding the Thương Tang Kính. In 1062 he settled in Đàm Ảnh Thành, and he has listened to the pool ever since.
places.art_brief: A city miniature on a flat grassy shore at a river mouth: low rectangular grey walls, grey-tile roofs, a small river quay. At the centre a large perfectly round pool, mirror-still, reflecting sky and clouds, ringed by small open pavilions with upturned grey roofs. Warm golden light from the top left, the pool a disc of pale gold and blue. No text, no people larger than specks, no seaward harbour quays, nothing outside the walls.
levels: A painters' hall with long open galleries rises on the pool's north side, and the river quay is rebuilt in stone.
A second walled ward takes in the river's far bank, and a tall pavilion over the water is built so its reflection completes it in the pool.

places.name: Tương Phùng Thị
places.look: A market built half on the water at the quay below Bình Thủy Môn: boats lashed side by side into a floating raft of stalls that rises and falls with the tide. Planks run between them, and faded green awnings drift like duckweed on the strait.
places.lore: The market grew beside Bình Thủy Môn in 525 and has never had a fixed shape; boats join and leave, and no stall sits in the same place two days running. It is said that anyone looking for a lost friend need only wait long enough at Tương Phùng Thị, and the strait ferries leave from its outer boats.
places.art_brief: A market miniature on calm coastal water: a loose, irregular raft of many small boats lashed together, joined by planks, each with a tiny faded green or ochre awning, against a short stone quay with a few grey-tile sheds. Turquoise water, warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, no sect halls, nothing outside the quay and the raft.
levels: A stone quay with warehouses anchors the raft, and the boats spread into two lashed arms.
A covered market hall stands on piles over the water, and the raft rings it in a wide floating crescent.

places.name: Xích Ngạn Trấn
places.look: A small walled town atop red cliffs on the island's east coast, its grey roofs bright against the rust-red rock. A long stair cut into the cliff face zigzags down to a cove where the boats are drawn up.
places.lore: The first mainland traders named the red cliffs Xích Ngạn in 330, and the town that grew on top kept the name. Its people grind the red rock into a pigment for the island's sails, and a Xích Ngạn boat is known far out at sea by its rust-coloured canvas.
places.art_brief: A town miniature on a grassy clifftop: a small rectangular grey wall and grey-tile roofs at the edge of a sheer rust-red sandstone cliff; a zigzag stair cut into the cliff face down to a tiny cove with boats with red-brown sails drawn up on the shingle. Warm golden light from the top left glowing on the red rock. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the clifftop and the cove.
levels: A pigment mill and drying yard sit inside the walls, and a second stair is cut to a new landing.
The town fills the clifftop, a stone pier runs out from the cove, and a tall grey-tile hall overlooks the sea from the cliff edge.

places.name: Hải Yến Trấn
places.look: A fishing town of low grey roofs on the flat island shore. Every house wears deep double eaves, and under them the sea swallows' nests cluster so thickly that the eaves look whitewashed; at dusk the air above the town is a whirl of birds.
places.lore: Since the Age of the North Star Compact the people of Hải Yến have sold swallows' nests to alchemists (đan sư), who prize them for pills that clear the breath. Families own eaves the way others own fields, and a daughter's dowry is counted in nests. Harvesters take only the nests the birds have left.
places.art_brief: A low town miniature on a flat grassy shore: a small rectangular wall, grey-tile roofs each with deep double eaves, the undersides crusted pale white with nests, a cloud of tiny dark specks of birds over the roofs. A small harbour of fishing boats. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the walls and harbour.
levels: Tall nest houses with many tiers of eaves rise inside the walls, and the harbour gains a stone quay.
A ring of nest towers stands along the walls, and a nest market hall with a high grey roof faces the harbour.

places.name: Triều Âm Thành
places.look: A walled city on the island's western shore at a river mouth, grey roofs stepping up from the water. Along its sea front runs a stone breakwater bored with round holes that moan and sing as the tide pushes through.
places.lore: Lạc Hà Tông founded the city in 540 as its western foothold on Cô Vụ Đảo. Its people tell time by the breakwater's note, low at the ebb and high at the flood, and its watchmen call the tide instead of the hour. Musicians from the mainland come to tune to it, and the children call the sound the island breathing.
places.history: A generation before the city, Cô Vụ Đảo became Lạc Hà Tông's land under the Strait Oath. In 540 Lạc Hà founded Triều Âm Thành on the island's western shore, where a river meets the sea, as a harbour of its own beside the old Cô Phàm ports. Its builders bored the breakwater so the tide would pass through rather than break it, found that it sang, and named the city for the sound. When the Cô Phàm fleet was lost in the Age of the North Star Compact, Triều Âm's harbour took much of the island's sea trade. In the great storm of the Age of Vein Wars, while the fishing fleet sheltered at Nguyệt Loan Thôn, the breakwater is said to have shrieked all night and held. Lạc Hà's ships to and from the island still call here first.
places.art_brief: A city miniature on a flat western shore at a river mouth: rectangular grey walls, grey-tile roofs stepping up gently from the water, a harbour of ships. Along the sea front a long curved stone breakwater pierced with rows of round holes, white spray bursting through them. Warm golden light from the top left, blue-green sea. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the walls and breakwater.
levels: The breakwater is lengthened along the river mouth and a customs hall rises at the harbour gate.
A second harbour basin is walled in, and a tall bell-less listening tower stands on the breakwater's end, open to the sea wind.

places.name: Bối Sa Thôn
places.look: A fishing village on a gleaming white beach on the island's grassy coast. On the sand above the tide line stands a small mound-shrine built entirely of white shells, with the village's drying mats spread around it.
places.lore: Since the Age of First Gates (Khai Môn Kỷ) the islanders have gathered shells on Bối Sa's beach to trade as coins on the mainland, long before any sect held the island. Old shell money is still taken in the village for small things, and every child adds a shell to the shrine on its first birthday.
places.art_brief: A small village miniature on a bright white beach: a few low grey-tile roofs behind the dune grass, rectangles of drying mats on the sand, and above the tide line a small rounded mound of white shells with a tiny roofed niche. Turquoise shallows. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the beach and village.
levels: A shell-sorting shed and a boat slip are added, and the shrine is given a low stone ring.
The village grows a short stone quay and a small hall for the shell traders, and the shrine mound rises higher every year.

places.name: Lãng Thạch Thôn
places.look: A small village behind a sea stack on the island coast. The stack, Wave Rock, stands split in two from crown to waterline, and through the gap shows the dark mouth of a sea cave.
places.lore: Wave Rock split in a storm in 960 and opened a sea cave full of old charts drawn by the lost sailors of Cô Phàm Các. The village answers to Bình Thủy Môn, and its fishers still row visitors into the cave; rumour says not every chart was carried out.
places.art_brief: A small village miniature on a grassy coast: a few grey-tile roofs and boats on the shingle, and just offshore a tall dark sea stack cleanly split into two halves, a black cave mouth visible in the gap at the waterline. White surf at its base. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the village and the stack.
levels: A landing stage is built at the cave mouth and a chart-copiers' hut rises in the village.
The village gains a small walled yard and a stone jetty reaching toward the split rock.

places.name: Dương Liễu Thôn
places.look: A village on the island's dunes, its grey roofs sheltered behind long rows of wind-bent willows planted along the sand ridges. Their roots bind the dunes, and from the sea the village looks hedged in green.
places.lore: Since 750 the villagers have planted willows on the dunes to hold the island's sand against the storms. Each household tends its own row, and a newborn's cord is buried at the foot of a new willow.
places.art_brief: A small village miniature on pale sand dunes: a few grey-tile roofs in the hollows, with long parallel rows of leaning green willows on the dune ridges between village and sea. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the dunes.
levels: New willow rows run along the outer dunes and a boat shed is built in their lee.
A wattle sea fence stretches behind the willows, and a small grey-tile hall stands on the highest dune.

places.name: Tình Sa Thôn
places.look: A village of low grey roofs on a broad, sunny sandbar at a river mouth. On the bar lies a long driftwood effigy of a whale, built by the villagers and weathered silver.
places.lore: In 1190 a whale stranded on Tình Sa's sunny sands lived three days while the islanders worked to give it back to the sea. The villagers built the driftwood whale to remember it, and mend it from new driftwood whenever a storm takes a piece.
places.art_brief: A small village miniature on a golden sandbar at a river mouth: a few low grey-tile roofs, boats in the river channel, and on the open sand a long whale shape made of silver-grey driftwood. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the sandbar.
levels: A fish-drying frame and a jetty into the river channel are added.
The village spreads along both banks of the river mouth, joined by a plank footbridge, and a small shrine roof shelters the whale's head.

places.name: Nguyệt Loan Thôn
places.look: A fishing village around a perfect crescent cove, its arms of rock nearly closing at the mouth. Inside rides a crowded fleet of island boats, their masts thick as reeds.
places.lore: In the great storm of 870 the moon-shaped cove sheltered the island's fishing fleet, and boats from every harbour on Cô Vụ Đảo still run for Nguyệt Loan when the sky turns. Captains who ride out a storm here hang a carved wooden moon on the village boat shed in thanks.
places.art_brief: A small village miniature around a crescent-shaped cove whose rocky arms almost close: grey-tile roofs along the curved shore, the still water inside crowded with many tiny boats and masts. Warm golden light from the top left, calm water inside, white surf outside. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the cove.
levels: A storm wall is built along the cove's curve and a long boat shed rises at its head.
Mooring piers ring the cove, and a small grey-tile storm shrine stands on the tip of one rocky arm.

places.name: Bích Không Cảng
places.look: The empty harbour below Đàm Ảnh Thành: long stone quays running out into blue water, lined with bare mooring posts and not one boat. At the root of the quays stands the roofless shell of a great sail loft, its rafters open to the sky.
places.lore: From here the sails of Cô Phàm Các vanished into the blue, and here the fleet failed to come home. Giang Bích Không made the Viễn Ảnh Châm for this harbour, a needle that always points to the last ship to leave port. The widows left a year after the loss and the quays have faced the empty sea since; fishers will not tie up here, and say the needle, wherever it is now, still points out past the harbour mouth.
places.history: Cô Phàm Các, founded on Cô Vụ Đảo by Giang Bích Không in the Age of Seven Seats, built the harbour of Bích Không Cảng below Đàm Ảnh Thành soon after. In 420 Giang Bích Không made the Viễn Ảnh Châm, a needle that always points to the last ship to leave port, and his sailors read the sea like a scripture. At the close of that age the Strait Oath bound the sect to Lạc Hà Tông, and Lạc Hà's cargoes sailed from these quays too. In the Age of the North Star Compact a storm sank the whole fleet with its head Mã Viễn Ảnh, and the Pavilion of the Lone Sail was lost at sea. In 706 the widows of Bích Không Cảng left the harbour, and the empty quays have faced the blue ever since. Lạc Hà holds the ruin and has never refitted it. What became of the needle is not recorded.
places.art_brief: A ruin miniature on a grassy shore: long straight stone quays running out into deep blue water, lined with rows of small bare mooring posts, no boats; at their landward end the tall roofless shell of a timber-and-stone sail loft, bare rafters standing as broken verticals. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people, no intact roofs, nothing outside the quays and the loft.

places.name: Vụ Báo Lâm
places.look: A steaming jungle in the island's interior, its canopy drowned in white mist most mornings. Out of the mist rises a single black rock outcrop, where the leopards bask when the sun burns through.
places.lore: Mist leopards hunt here, grey-spotted and nearly invisible in the fog; islanders say you hear one only after it has passed you. No sect holds the jungle, and Bình Thủy's ferrymen warn travellers off the inland paths.
places.art_brief: A natural site: a dense green jungle canopy half buried in soft white mist, with one dark basalt outcrop rising clear above it. No buildings, no roofline. Warm golden light from the top left on the rock and the mist tops. No text, no creatures larger than specks, nothing outside the jungle patch.

places.name: Mục Vân Trang
places.look: A manor seat on a low rise near the coast of the open plain, its halls climbing in tiers to a tall stable tower under a sweeping grey roof. Around the foot of the rise runs a great oval racing track of packed earth, and on it pale spirit horses (linh mã) move like clouds.
places.lore: Herders of the open plain founded Mục Vân Trang in 740 to raise spirit horses that run like clouds under the endless sky of Trường Thiên Nguyên. It is sworn to Lạc Hà Tông and its body cultivators train with their beasts, riders and horses together. Its head, Khấu Mục Vân, was born in Thanh Điền the same night as a spirit foal that would let no one else ride it. Its horses won every race at the Lạc Hà festival of 1185, and Kim Vạn Lý, who bet on them, lost anyway; how is still argued in every tavern on the plain.
places.history: Lạc Hà Tông extended its rule over the open grassland of Trường Thiên Nguyên in the Age of Seven Seats, and the herders of the plain kept their flocks under it. In 740 herders founded Mục Vân Trang to raise spirit horses that run like clouds. As its herds grew, the manor took the villages of Thanh Điền, Điền Viên and Chu Tân under its hand. In 940 Khấu Mục Vân was born in Thanh Điền, and a spirit foal born the same night would let no one else ride it; he leads the manor now. Its horses became the pride of the plain, ridden by Lạc Hà's couriers across the grassland. In 1185 Mục Vân Trang's horses won every race at the Lạc Hà festival, and Kim Vạn Lý bet on them and lost anyway. The track below the manor has never been busier.
places.art_brief: A vertical sect seat on a low grassy rise near the sea: grey-tile roofs over red-brown timber halls climbing in tiers to a tall stable tower with a broad sweeping grey roof, the tallest outline on the plain. Around the base a wide oval track of pale packed earth with tiny white specks of horses, and low paddock fences. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the rise and the track.
levels: A second stable hall and a long covered viewing gallery rise beside the track.
The manor climbs to a high riders' hall above the stable tower, and a second track loops out toward the coast with stone stands.

places.name: Nhạn Thanh Thành
places.look: A walled city where a river meets the sea on the dry steppe coast, its grey roofs crowded around wool warehouses. Over the main gate rises a tower whose two upswept roofs spread like the wings of a goose in flight, and the wild geese pass over it in long formations each autumn.
places.lore: Lạc Hà Tông founded the city in 450 where the wild geese fly in formation, and it is the wool market of the western plain; Kim Vạn Lý, the richest merchant of the west, made his name here. Since the cold year of 1120, when archers shot the low-flying geese from the walls, no one may shoot a goose in the city. Its scholars retire to Điền Viên Thôn to farm.
places.history: Lạc Hà Tông took the open grassland of Trường Thiên Nguyên in the Age of Seven Seats, and in 450 founded Nhạn Thanh Thành on the western plain where the wild geese fly in formation. The city grew on the plain's wool and grain, shipped from its river harbour. By the Age of Vein Wars its scholars were retiring to farm the gardens and fields of Điền Viên Thôn, which fed the city. In 1040 Kim Vạn Lý bought the wool of the whole plain in one season and became the richest merchant of the west. In 1120 the wild geese flew so low over the city in a cold year that archers shot them from the walls, and the city forbade it ever after. Kim Vạn Lý still lives here, and the goose gate is the first thing the herders see when they drive their flocks to market.
places.art_brief: A city miniature on a dry, tawny steppe coast at a river mouth: rectangular grey walls, grey-tile roofs and long low warehouse roofs, a river harbour with boats. Over the main gate a tower with two broad roofs swept sharply upward like spread wings, the tallest outline. A thin V of tiny geese in the sky above it. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the walls and harbour.
levels: A great wool exchange with a long grey roof rises by the harbour, and the walls take in the dyers' quarter.
A second winged tower is raised over the river gate, and stone wool warehouses line both banks to the sea.

places.name: Thanh Điền Trấn
places.look: A small walled market town in a sea of bright green fields that run to the horizon. Outside its gate stretches a long row of hitching rails where the farmers' horses wait, since the fields are too far to walk.
places.lore: The fields around Thanh Điền stretch so far that its farmers ride to work, and children learn to sit a horse before they can walk far. The town answers to Mục Vân Trang, whose head Khấu Mục Vân was born here in 940 on the same night as a spirit foal; the town still holds a horse fair on that night.
places.art_brief: A low town miniature in flat, vivid green fields: a small rectangular grey wall and grey-tile roofs, and outside the gate a long straight row of timber hitching rails with tiny horse specks. Green field strips running out to the edges of the footprint, the coast just at one side. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the town and its near fields.
levels: A walled horse yard joins the town and the hitching rails double along the road.
A granary row and a fair ground with a viewing stand rise beside the walls.

places.name: Thảo Đường Thành
places.look: A walled city on the flat coastal plain, its grey roofs low among farms. Outside the walls lies a chequerboard of grass-banked ponds, each a square of sky, with fish and ducks raised in every one.
places.lore: Lạc Hà Tông founded the city in 680 among the farms of the western plain, and it lives by them: rice, fish ponds, ducks and hemp. Its name comes from the ponds the first farmers dug; each family owns a square, and the banks between are common ground. Its market day is the slowest and friendliest on the plain.
places.history: Farmers worked this stretch of the western plain long before the city, under Lạc Hà Tông's rule since the Age of Seven Seats. They dug grass-banked ponds for fish and ducks and to catch the plain's floods before they reached the fields. In 680 Lạc Hà founded Thảo Đường Thành among the farms, to gather their harvest and guard them. Through the wars of the Compact age its fields and ponds kept the western plain fed. During the War of Broken Halberds Lạc Hà built its western watch at Lô Cảng Thôn to guard the coast boats along this shore. Today the sect's stewards come here to count harvests, not swords.
places.art_brief: A city miniature on a flat green coastal plain: rectangular grey walls, low grey-tile roofs, and outside the walls a regular grid of square ponds with green grass banks, each pond a small square of reflected blue sky, tiny white specks of ducks. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the walls and the pond grid.
levels: A new granary ward is walled in and more ponds are dug in rows along the road.
A tall grain hall with a double roof rises at the city's heart, and canals link the pond grid to the sea.

places.name: Ngư Lương Trấn
places.look: A small walled town where a plain river spills into the sea. Across the river mouth runs a great zigzag weir of stone and bamboo, the largest on the plain, its traps glinting with fish.
places.lore: Lạc Hà's rule brought fishing weirs to the plain's rivers in 430, and the town grew around the largest. The weir is rebuilt piece by piece every year, the family that tends a stretch of it keeps that stretch's fish, and quarrels over the weir go to the town's oldest fisher.
places.art_brief: A low town miniature at a river mouth on a flat grassy coast: a small rectangular grey wall and grey-tile roofs on one bank; across the river mouth a long zigzag line of stones and bamboo fencing with small basket traps. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the town and the weir.
levels: A fish market roof and smoking sheds rise on the bank by the weir.
A second weir is built upstream and the walls take in both banks, joined by a footbridge along the old weir.

places.name: Điền Viên Thôn
places.look: A village of gardens and fields on the plain coast, its grey roofs half hidden by orchard walls. In nearly every garden wall is a round moon gate, and through them show the small studies of retired scholars.
places.lore: Since 890 the gardens and fields of Điền Viên have fed the scholars of Nhạn Thanh Thành, who retire here to farm. The village answers to Mục Vân Trang, and its old scholars write letters for the herders and are paid in vegetables.
places.art_brief: A small village miniature on a green coastal plain: a few grey-tile roofs inside whitewashed garden walls, each wall pierced by a round moon gate, neat vegetable plots and fruit trees inside. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the gardens.
levels: A small library pavilion and a shared orchard are added.
A walled scholars' garden with a pond pavilion forms the heart of the village, and new moon gates open onto the fields.

places.name: Yến Quy Thôn
places.look: A small farm village on the plain coast, its grey roofs gathered around one old farmstead. The old farm's roof ridge is lined end to end with little clay swallows, and the real birds perch among them.
places.lore: Swallows returned to the same farm every spring for a hundred years, and by 300 the village was named Yến Quy, Swallows' Return. The farm still stands; each family adds a clay swallow to its ridge, and a year when the real birds are late is a year to plant carefully.
places.art_brief: A small village miniature on a green coastal plain: a few grey-tile roofs around one larger old farmhouse whose long roof ridge is lined with a row of tiny dark clay bird figures. Fields and a farm pond around it. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the village.
levels: A new barn and a threshing floor are built beside the old farm.
The village grows a small walled yard and a shrine hall, its ridge also lined with clay swallows.

places.name: Chu Tân Thôn
places.look: A ferry village on the low, wet shore, below the level of the sea at high tide. Two tall carved ferry posts stand at the old ford, joined by a heavy rope across a narrow tidal creek, with a flat barge crawling along it.
places.lore: A ford on the plain's widest river became Chu Tân Thôn in 520; the river has since wandered from the village, but the old ford's posts still stand, and at high tide the villagers haul travellers across the creek on the rope ferry. The village answers to Mục Vân Trang, whose herds cross here every spring, and the ferrymen know each horse by name.
places.art_brief: A small village miniature on low, wet coastal flats: a few grey-tile roofs beside a narrow tidal creek, two tall carved dark posts on either side of it joined by a taut rope, a flat barge on the water between. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, no river, nothing outside the flats.
levels: A ferry inn and a holding pen for herds are built by the landing.
A second rope and barge are added, and a small walled waystation stands on the far bank.

places.name: Lô Cảng Thôn
places.look: A village of reed-thatched boat sheds around a sheltered reed harbour on the plain coast. Out of the reeds rises a tall timber watchtower flying Lạc Hà's sunset-red banner, the sect's western watch.
places.lore: The reed harbour at Lô Cảng shelters the coast boats from the open sea, and in 800 Lạc Hà Tông built its western watch here. Watchmen and fishers share the village, and the tower lights a fire when strange sails are seen.
places.art_brief: A small village miniature on a reedy coast: a few grey-tile houses and long reed-thatched boat sheds around a small sheltered pool among tall reeds; one tall timber watchtower with a small red banner rising above it all. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the reed harbour.
levels: A walled barracks yard joins the watchtower and a jetty runs through the reeds.
A stone signal platform tops the tower, and a second harbour pool is cut into the reeds.

places.name: Diêm Điền Thôn
places.look: A village at the edge of a vast glittering grid of salt pans on the flat west coast. Between the shallow white squares stand rows of shining salt cones, raked up by hand.
places.lore: Salt pans dug at Diêm Điền in 200 made the continent's first sea salt, before any great sect held the west. The salt-makers keep the first pan unused and fenced, and pour a handful of new salt into it every year.
places.art_brief: A small village miniature on a flat coast: a few grey-tile roofs beside a wide grid of shallow rectangular pans, white and pale pink, with rows of small bright white salt cones on the dykes. Warm golden light from the top left glinting on the salt. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the pans.
levels: A salt store with a high grey roof rises and the pans spread along the shore.
A walled salt yard and a stone loading jetty serve the pans.

places.name: Phù Chử Đảo
places.look: A low wooded isle off the plain coast, its trees dark against the water. Around it floats a thick, shifting raft of wild ducks, so dense the water looks feathered.
places.lore: The isle takes its name from the old line about crane shoals and wild-duck isles. Since the Age of Seven Seats boats have had to wait for the ducks to move before they can land, and fishers say anyone who forces a way through will have no luck all season. No sect holds it, and only egg-gatherers go ashore in spring.
places.history: The isle had no name in any record before the fishers of the western plain began to row out to it. When Lạc Hà Tông took the grassland of Trường Thiên Nguyên early in the Age of Seven Seats, the isle was left outside its rule, too small to claim. By 470 wild ducks crowded Phù Chử so thickly that boats had to wait for them to move. Egg-gatherers from the coast villages row out every spring and take care to leave most nests. Hunters who shot into the flocks, the coast says, found the ducks gone the next year, and no one hunts there now. No sect has claimed the isle in any age.
places.art_brief: A natural site: a small low island covered in dark temperate trees, with a narrow pale shore, ringed on the water by a dense brown-and-white mass of tiny duck specks. No buildings, no roofline. Warm golden light from the top left, calm blue water. No text, no people, nothing outside the isle and its ring of birds.

places.name: Tịch Chiếu Đảo
places.look: The westernmost island, a low grassy hump in the open sea. On its western cliff stands a single long stone bench facing the sunset, and behind it the grass is dotted with small cairns of grey stones.
places.lore: Tịch Chiếu is the last land to see the sunset of Lạc Hà, and since the Age of the North Star Compact the sect's elders have gone there to die. They sit on the bench at evening; the cairns mark those who did not come back. The boats that bring them out do not wait.
places.history: Tịch Chiếu Đảo lies west of all other land, the last to see the sun go down over Lạc Hà Tông's western lands. No settlement has ever stood on it. Lạc Hà, founded late in the Age of First Gates in the western lands where the sun goes down, named it for the evening glow. By 600 the sect's elders had begun to go there to die, sailing out at the end of their lives to watch the last sunset. Each leaves a small cairn of grey stones on the grass. The island is held by no one, and fishers give it a wide berth out of respect. Elders who feel their time near still ask for a boat to Tịch Chiếu.
places.art_brief: A natural site: a small low grassy island with a short western cliff, a single long grey stone bench at the cliff edge facing away to the west, and scattered tiny cairns of grey stones on the grass behind. No buildings, no roofline. Warm golden light from the top left, the sea turning amber. No text, no people, nothing outside the island.

places.name: Thiên Bảo Trai
places.look: A tall sect seat on a dry steppe rise above the bay, its stacked pagoda roofs ridged in gilt bronze that burns in the evening sun. Around its base a ring of refining furnace chimneys trails thin smoke in green, copper and violet.
places.lore: Founded in 350 as a refiners' workshop beside the bay, Thiên Bảo Trai refines artifacts (luyện khí) and runs the treasure market of Thu Thủy Loan, sworn to Lạc Hà Tông; its sign still reads that the riches of the land are heaven's treasures. Since Phan Vật Hoa became mistress in 1050 it holds a treasure auction every season. Buyers sit behind screens and bid by bell, so no one knows who bought what.
places.history: Thiên Bảo Trai was founded beside the bay in 350 as a refiners' workshop, its sign declaring the riches of the land heaven's treasures. In 360 red gold was found at Xích Kim, and the workshop bought the mine before Lạc Hà's stewards heard of it. By 500 a market for the land's riches, Vật Hoa Thị, had grown beside it. In 700 its refiners were washing their finest work in the clear brooks of Khê Đầu and Khê Thanh. When Kim Cốc Viên collapsed and its city burned, the Trai hired, in 1004, the ruined merchants who could still count. In 1050 Phan Vật Hoa became mistress and began a treasure auction every season. In 1180 a buyer from Thiên Bảo Trai bought a white bear brought alive out of Vô Tung Lâm at Mộc Lan Thành, and the Trai's reach now runs from the frost coast to the bay.
places.art_brief: A vertical sect seat on a dry tawny rise: stacked pagoda roofs of grey tile with bright gilt-bronze ridges and finials, the tallest outline in the land, over terraces of pale stone. Around the base a ring of short brick furnace chimneys trailing faint wisps of green, copper and violet smoke. The bay a glint at one edge. Warm golden light from the top left catching the gilt. No text, no people larger than specks, no market stalls, nothing outside the rise.
levels: An auction hall with a gilded double roof rises on a new terrace, and the furnace ring grows a second row.
The pagoda gains a higher tier with a gilt spire, and a walled treasury court with its own gate faces the market road.

places.name: Tử Điện Thành
places.look: A walled port city on the bay where a river meets the sea, its grey roofs packed tight inside strong walls. Above them rises a tall armoury tower roofed in violet-glazed tile, and on clear evenings the faint violet shimmer of its ward array (trận pháp) hangs over the whole city.
places.lore: Lạc Anh Phái founded the city on the bay side of the Petal Shore in 360; Lạc Hà Tông took it by the Pivot's judgement in 620 and renamed it Tử Điện Thành for its armoury, after the purple-lightning sword Tử Điện. Its smiths and guards are the most disciplined in the bay. Old families still plant a peach tree in the courtyard for Lạc Anh, though the city's first name is all but forgotten.
places.history: Lạc Anh Phái founded a city on the bay side of the Petal Shore in 360; it would bear another name before it bore its last. The same year Lạc Hà Tông forged twin swords for its armoury, Tử Điện and Thanh Sương, after the purple lightning and blue frost of an old general's blades. Two and a half centuries later Lạc Anh Phái split over its inheritance and its last head, Khương Vọng Nguyệt, vanished. Lạc Hà and Thính Vũ Lâu both claimed the empty Petal Shore, their disciples fought in the burning orchards, and Hồng Vũ Thành burned. In 620 the Pivot's judgement gave the bay to Lạc Hà and the forest to Thính Vũ, and Lạc Hà renamed the bay city Tử Điện Thành, for its armoury; it raised a ward array so the fire would not come twice. In the War of Broken Halberds Thanh Sương fell from its bearer's hand on Chiết Kích Nguyên, and no one has dared go back for it. Late in the Age of Vein Wars Tô Vãn Chiếu became head of Lạc Hà Tông and took the sword Tử Điện.
places.art_brief: A city miniature on a bay shore at a river mouth: strong rectangular grey walls, dense grey-tile roofs, a busy harbour. Above them a tall square armoury tower with several roofs of glazed violet-purple tile, the tallest point; a barely visible pale violet dome of light over the walls. A few pink peach trees in courtyards. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the walls and harbour.
levels: A second armoury hall with violet tile rises inside a new inner wall, and the harbour gains a war-boat slip.
The walls are doubled on the landward side with gate towers, and the ward array's shimmer brightens into a clear violet dome over the bay front.

places.name: Vật Hoa Thị
places.look: A busy open market on the dry steppe below Thiên Bảo Trai, rows of awnings around a central square. In the square stands a great bronze steelyard on a stone frame, taller than a house, where any trader may have goods weighed in public.
places.lore: The market of the land's riches grew beside Thiên Bảo Trai in 500 and sells what the Trai refines and what the bay digs, grows and catches. Its public scale is the market's law: a deal weighed there cannot be undone. The famous alchemist Lạc Đan Thanh has kept a pill stall here since 1110 and charges whatever he likes.
places.history: In 500 a market for the land's riches grew beside Thiên Bảo Trai and was called Vật Hoa Thị. It sold the Trai's refinings and the red gold of Xích Kim, and drew traders from all round Thu Thủy Loan. In 1004, a year after Kim Cốc burned, Kim Cốc's merchants came begging here, and Thiên Bảo Trai hired the ones who could still count. The traders say the great scale was set up in the square after the crash, to keep the market honest. In 1105 Lạc Đan Thanh bought the Đào Nguyên Đồ, the only map of the way into the fisherman's lost valley, here for a pill no one else could make. In 1110 he set up his pill stall in Vật Hoa Thị, and he has charged whatever he likes ever since. Who sold him the painting is not recorded.
places.art_brief: A market miniature on a dry tawny plain: a low walled square of grey-tile stall roofs and striped ochre and dull red awnings, with a large dark bronze steelyard beam on a tall stone frame at the centre, the tallest element. A road leading off toward a rise. Warm golden light from the top left glinting on the bronze. No text, no people larger than specks, no sect pagoda, nothing outside the market walls.
levels: A covered arcade rings the square and a caravan yard is walled in beside the road.
A stone exchange hall with a high double roof faces the scale, and the market's walls take in a second square.

places.name: Liễu Ngạn Trấn
places.look: A small walled town on a river through flat grassland, set behind a high earthen levee. On the levee stands a tall stone flood-pillar cut with the marks of every great flood, the highest painted red; willows line the bank on either side.
places.lore: In 410 the townsfolk planted willows on the bank at Liễu Ngạn to hold the river where it floods, and the town has fought the river ever since. When the water climbs past the red mark on the pillar, the drum is beaten and every household sends someone to the levee.
places.art_brief: A low town miniature on a flat green riverbank: a small rectangular grey wall and grey-tile roofs behind a long raised earthen levee lined with willows; on the levee a single tall slim stone pillar with dark notches and one red band. The river running past. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the town and levee.
levels: The levee is faced with stone and a drum house is built beside the flood-pillar.
A stone river gate and a sluice tower guard the town, and the levee runs on past the walls on both sides.

places.name: Hòa Phong Trấn
places.look: A small port town on the open bay coast, its grey roofs low and airy. On every roof stands a tall woven wind-scoop turned toward the sea, so the whole town seems to lean into the breeze.
places.lore: In 900, the year of the southern plague, a gentle sea breeze kept Hòa Phong Trấn free of fever, and the town has built wind-scoops on its roofs ever since to keep the sea air moving through every room. Sick travellers are brought here to recover, and its healers swear by the breeze before any pill.
places.art_brief: A low town miniature on a grassy bay coast: a small rectangular wall, grey-tile roofs each topped by a tall woven straw-coloured scoop opening toward the sea, a small harbour. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the walls and harbour.
levels: A house of healing with a long open veranda rises facing the sea.
The town grows a seaside terrace of guesthouses for the sick, each with its own tall wind-scoop, and a stone quay for the boats that bring them.

places.name: Ngũ Cốc Thành
places.look: A walled port city on the bay coast, its quay lined with granaries. Along the waterfront stands a row of tall round grain towers, each roofed differently for its grain, with wooden chutes running down to the ships.
places.lore: Ngũ Cốc Thành grew rich on the trade Kim Cốc lost when Kim Cốc Viên burned. It ships the grain of the bay and the western plain, and many of its merchants are Kim Cốc families who rebuilt their fortunes in grain. Each grain tower has its own guild, and their rivalry runs the city.
places.history: Before this city, much of the bay's trade went through Kim Cốc Thành, the merchant city around Kim Cốc Viên. A few years before this city was founded, Kim Cốc Viên collapsed in a market crash and a great fire, and Kim Cốc Thành burned. Its merchants were begging in Vật Hoa Thị the next year, and its trade looked for a new harbour. In 1010 Ngũ Cốc Thành was founded on the bay coast and grew rich on the trade Kim Cốc lost. Its builders raised the grain towers on the quay first and the walls after, so the trade would never wait. Under Lạc Hà Tông it is now the bay's grain port, and its guilds, remembering Kim Cốc's fire, keep their granaries in stone.
places.art_brief: A city miniature on a flat bay coast: rectangular grey walls, grey-tile roofs, and along the quay a line of tall round stone-and-timber grain towers with conical roofs in grey tile, thatch and red-brown tile, wooden chutes slanting to ships at the quay. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the walls and quay.
levels: A guild hall for the grain towers rises behind the quay, and a breakwater shelters the ships.
A second row of grain towers is built on a new pier, and the walls take in the barge canal from the plain.

places.name: Khê Thanh Thôn
places.look: A village on a clear grassland brook, its grey roofs strung along the water. Over the brook stand a row of small covered rinsing sheds on stilts, where the water chatters loudly over the stones beneath them.
places.lore: The brook at Khê Thanh runs so clear that since 700 Thiên Bảo Trai has washed its finest refinings in it. The Trai's apprentices come down with covered baskets, the villagers are paid to keep the banks free of mud and cattle, and the brook's chatter is said to sing the flaws out of the metal.
places.art_brief: A small village miniature on a clear, shallow, stony brook in green grassland: a few grey-tile houses along the bank and a row of small grey-roofed sheds standing on stilts over the water. Warm golden light from the top left sparkling on the brook. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the brook's banks.
levels: More rinsing sheds are built downstream and a small inspection hall for the Trai's stewards rises on the bank.
A walled storehouse for refinings and a stone footbridge join the village across the brook.

places.name: Khê Đầu Thôn
places.look: A small village at the head of a brook on the grassland, where the water rises from the ground. The spring pours from a stone spout carved as a carp's head into a round basin, and the brook starts from its overflow.
places.lore: Khê Đầu sits where the brook begins, upstream of Khê Thanh, and its water is the clearest of all; Thiên Bảo Trai washes its finest refinings at both villages. The villagers guard the spring like a shrine and let no one wash in the basin itself, only below it.
places.art_brief: A small village miniature on gently rising grassland: a few grey-tile roofs around a round stone basin fed by a carved stone carp-head spout, the clear brook spilling out of it and away. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the village.
levels: A low wall and a small roof are built around the spring basin.
A spring hall with a grey-tile roof shelters the carp spout, and a stone channel leads the brook toward Khê Thanh.

places.name: Hải Môn Thôn
places.look: A fishing village on the bay coast beside a great natural rock arch, the Sea Gate. Twice a day the tide runs through the arch in a white rush, and the village boats wait on the inner side for the slack.
places.lore: Since 450 the village has been named for its Sea Gate, the rock arch the tide runs through twice a day. Fishers time everything by it, and a bride and groom row through the arch at slack water for luck.
places.art_brief: A small village miniature on a grassy coast: a few grey-tile roofs and boats on the shore inside a sheltered pool, beside a large natural stone arch standing in the sea with white water rushing through it. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the village and the arch.
levels: A boat shed and a stone landing are built inside the arch's shelter.
A small grey-tile shrine stands on the arch's landward foot, and a jetty reaches out to the slack-water channel.

places.name: Tân Khẩu Thôn
places.look: A village at the mouth of a harbour on the bay coast, its houses all facing the sea. On the landward side they join into one long blank wall with no windows, turned against the plain.
places.lore: Refugees from Vô Định Thành founded the village in 805 after the battle on the plain, and never speak of it; the blank wall says it for them. Their children are less careful: not long ago children of Tân Khẩu dared each other to touch the edge of the miasma (chướng khí) by Vô Định Thành, and one did not come back.
places.art_brief: A small village miniature at a harbour mouth on a grassy coast: grey-tile roofs in a row, their seaward sides open with doors and boats on the shore, their landward sides joined into one continuous blank grey wall. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the village.
levels: The village lengthens along the shore and a small fish market roof is built at the harbour mouth.
A stone quay and a lantern post mark the harbour mouth, and the blank wall is raised and capped in grey tile.

places.name: Xích Kim Khoáng
places.look: An open-cut mine in the dry badlands, its terraces cut into rock banded with streaks of red gold. At sunset the whole pit glows the colour of Lạc Hà's evening sky.
places.lore: Red gold was found here in 360, and Thiên Bảo Trai bought the mine before Lạc Hà's stewards heard of it; the Trai holds it still. Its gold goes to the treasure market and the refining furnaces, and miners say the seam runs redder the deeper it goes.
places.art_brief: A small mine miniature in eroded tan badlands: a stepped open pit with narrow terraces, its walls streaked with bands of glowing red-gold, a timber hoist and a couple of small grey-roofed sheds on the rim. Warm golden light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the pit and its rim.

places.name: Trường Hà Mạch
places.look: A high bare mountain on the border, its slope split by a long seam of amber-gold rock that winds down the face like a river. In the setting sun the seam glows as if the river ran with fire.
places.lore: Lạc Hà Tông found this spirit vein (linh mạch) on its new border with Thính Vũ Lâu in 620, the year the Petal Shore was divided, and named it for the line about the long river and the round setting sun. Its qi runs to earth and metal. Lạc Hà's disciples cultivate on its ledges with one eye on the far ridges, where Thính Vũ's land begins.
places.history: The mountain lay in no sect's reckoning until 620, when the Pivot's judgement divided the Petal Shore, the bay to Lạc Hà and the forest to Thính Vũ. That year Lạc Hà found the Long River vein on its new border with Thính Vũ and named it Trường Hà Mạch. On the eve of the War of Broken Halberds the founders of the two sects met on the Petal Shore and swore to end the Pivot's oversight, and through that war this border lay at the allies' backs, not their front. After the truce that ended it renewed the Compact, the two sects went back to watching each other. In the Age of Vein Wars, when neighbours fought short wars over the veins near their borders, Lạc Hà set a standing watch on the ridge; no war over this vein is recorded. Since Thính Vũ rebuilt its strength after Đan Sơn Mạch, the watch has been strengthened.
places.art_brief: A natural site: a steep, bare grey-brown high mountain face with a long winding seam of glowing amber-gold rock running down it like a river, a few tiny cultivation ledges cut beside it. No roofline. Warm golden light from the top left setting the seam alight. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the mountain face.

places.name: Kim Cốc Thành
